what_it_does: When a chip runs a neural network, it breaks large multiply-and-add computations into smaller pieces called partial sums — intermediate results that must be stored in memory and then retrieved to be added together later. Storing and fetching these partial sums in full 32-bit precision turns out to consume roughly 69% of the chip's power in typical AI accelerator designs. APSQ proposes compressing these partial sums down to 8-bit integers (a process called quantization — using smaller, rounded numbers) as they are computed, so far less data needs to be written to and read from memory. The approach groups partial sums intelligently and adds reconfigurable hardware logic so the compression is nearly lossless on models like BERT (a language model) and several image-processing networks. This co-design of the software algorithm and the physical hardware together achieves large power and bandwidth savings with negligible loss in model accuracy.
